days.learn: Architecture documentation: C4 diagrams and architecture decision records
days.title: Architecture diagram (C4 level 1-2) and 5 ADRs for your biggest decisions
days.doneWhen: `docs/architecture.md` shows a C4 level 1 and level 2 diagram that render on GitHub, and `docs/adr/` holds five ADRs, each with context, decision, alternatives and consequences
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Over 20 weeks you made dozens of decisions. Six months from now you will not remember why, and an interviewer will ask. A C4 diagram shows the system at the right zoom level for the audience; an architecture decision record (ADR) captures one decision with its context and trade-offs. Both turn a pile of code into a story a reviewer can follow in five minutes.

### What you'll build
On a new branch `release/v1.0`:
- `docs/architecture.md` with two diagrams in Mermaid (rendered by GitHub):
  - Level 1, context: the user, JobHunt, and external systems (email, company info service)
  - Level 2, containers: browser SPA, nginx, API, Hangfire inside the API, SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, Blob storage, the SMTP service, the trace collector
- Arrows labelled with protocol and purpose ("HTTPS JSON", "WebSocket push", "AMQP events")
- `docs/adr/0001-...md` to `0005-...md`, for example:
  - refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies, access tokens in memory (week 8)
  - outbox plus RabbitMQ instead of publishing in the request (week 17)
  - Hangfire instead of hosted services for scheduled work (week 14)
  - TanStack Query as the only client cache, updated by SignalR (weeks 5 and 15)
  - rowversion optimistic concurrency with 409 (week 10)
- A short template in `docs/adr/README.md` so future decisions follow the same shape

### Step by step
1. List the ten biggest decisions in JobHunt. Circle the five you would most like to be asked about.
2. Draw level 1 on paper first: one box for JobHunt, everything else around it.
3. Draw level 2: every container you deploy or depend on, and how they talk.
4. Write the diagrams in Mermaid and check they render in a GitHub preview.
5. Write each ADR in under a page: context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences (good and bad), status.
6. Link each ADR from the place in the code it affects, as a short comment.
7. Ask yourself the obvious challenge for each decision and add the answer to its consequences.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Both diagrams render and fit on one screen
- [ ] Every arrow has a label
- [ ] Each ADR lists at least one real alternative and one downside
- [ ] ADRs are numbered and dated
- [ ] A newcomer could explain the system from these docs alone

### Hints
- C4 has four levels; levels 1 and 2 are enough for most portfolio projects.
- ADRs are immutable: if you change your mind, write a new one that supersedes the old.
- "We chose X because the course said so" is not context. What problem did it solve for JobHunt?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  user([Job seeker]) -->|HTTPS| web[SPA via nginx]
  web -->|/api JSON, /hubs WebSocket| api[JobHunt API]
  %% TODO: SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, Blob, SMTP
```

### Common mistakes
- One giant diagram with every class in it.
- ADRs that only describe the decision, with no alternatives.
- Diagrams as images that go stale and cannot be diffed.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a level 3 component diagram for the API's layers.

### Check your understanding
- What does each C4 level show, and for whom?
- What makes an ADR useful years later?
- Which decision would you change today?

days.learn: Performance budgets: Lighthouse, API latency targets
days.title: Lighthouse and API latency pass; fix the two worst findings
days.doneWhen: Lighthouse scores (mobile profile) for the applications list and dashboard are recorded before and after, the two worst findings are fixed with measured gains, and p95 latency for list, detail and stats under a small load is written next to its target

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: ASP.NET Core built-in metrics

days.brief:
### Why this matters
"It feels fast on my laptop" is not a measurement. A performance budget turns speed into numbers you can defend: LCP, INP and CLS for the browser, p95 latency for the API. Measuring before and after each fix is how senior engineers talk about performance, and it gives you concrete numbers for your README and interviews.

### What you'll build
- A `PERFORMANCE.md` with budgets: LCP under 2.5 s, INP under 200 ms, CLS under 0.1 on a mid-range mobile profile; API p95 under 200 ms for list and detail, under 100 ms for cached stats
- Lighthouse runs (Chrome DevTools, mobile, incognito) against the production build from week 20, not the dev server
- API latency measured under a small load (a load testing tool of your choice, or a short script firing concurrent requests), read from the built-in request duration metric or your traces (week 16)
- Two fixes for the worst findings, each with before and after numbers. Typical candidates: an unindexed query (week 12 habits), an oversized bundle chunk, unoptimised images, render-blocking fonts, a missing cache header from nginx

### Step by step
1. Write the budgets first, so you cannot move the goalposts.
2. Run Lighthouse three times per page and take the median.
3. Read the diagnostics, not just the score. Note the two biggest opportunities.
4. Seed realistic data (week 12's generator) and load the API with a few concurrent users for a minute.
5. Find the slowest endpoint in the traces and look at its spans.
6. Fix one front-end and one back-end finding. Measure again the same way.
7. Record everything in `PERFORMANCE.md`.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Budgets are written before measuring
- [ ] Measurements use the production build and realistic data
- [ ] Each fix has before and after numbers
- [ ] p95 is reported, not the average
- [ ] Remaining gaps are listed honestly

### Hints
- Averages hide the slow requests users remember; p95 shows them.
- INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital; it measures responsiveness across the whole visit.
- Lighthouse runs on your machine; field data from real users can differ, and that is fine to mention.

```md
| Page / endpoint | Metric | Budget | Before | After |
| --------------- | ------ | ------ | ------ | ----- |
| /applications   | LCP    | 2.5 s  |        |       |
```

### Common mistakes
- Measuring the dev server.
- One run treated as truth.
- Optimising something that was not on the list of worst findings.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a Lighthouse run to CI that warns when a budget is exceeded.

### Check your understanding
- What do LCP, INP and CLS each measure?
- Why p95 instead of the average?
- What were your two worst findings and what did the fixes gain?

days.learn: Code review checklist; refactoring safely with tests
days.title: Self code review of both apps with a checklist; fix the top issues
days.doneWhen: A checklist of at least 15 review items lives in `docs/code-review.md`, both apps build with zero warnings and zero lint errors, and the top five findings are fixed in small commits with all tests green after each

learnLinks.label: GitHub Docs: About pull request reviews

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Twenty weeks of feature work leave rough edges: early code written before you knew better, TODOs, duplicated helpers. Reviewers judge a portfolio repo by its worst file. A written checklist makes review systematic instead of a mood, and your test suite from weeks 11 and 19 is what lets you refactor without fear. Many interviews include reviewing code; practising on your own is ideal preparation.

### What you'll build
- `docs/code-review.md`: a checklist grouped by correctness, security, data access, async and cancellation, errors, naming, React state, tests
- Example items: every query passes the `CancellationToken`; reads use `AsNoTracking`; no `.Result` or `.Wait()`; no magic strings for roles or cache keys; query keys come from the key factories; no state that could be derived; no `any`; every effect has the cleanup it needs; every endpoint has an ownership test
- Analyzers on: `AnalysisLevel` set to a recommended level and warnings treated as errors in Release, `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` passing
- Web: ESLint with zero warnings, `tsc --noEmit` clean, unused exports removed
- A findings list ranked by risk, and the top five fixed

### Step by step
1. Write the checklist from your own mistakes over the course, plus the review links.
2. Turn on the analyzers and fix or justify every warning. Suppressions need a comment.
3. Review the oldest code first (weeks 3 to 7): it was written before most of your patterns existed.
4. Search for `TODO`, `any`, `console.log`, `!` non-null assertions and commented-out code.
5. Rank findings: bugs and security first, then consistency, then style.
6. Fix the top five, one small commit each, running the relevant tests every time.
7. Leave the rest as issues with labels, so the repo shows how you would continue.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The checklist has at least 15 concrete, checkable items
- [ ] Zero build warnings and lint errors in both apps
- [ ] Each fix is a small commit with green tests
- [ ] No unexplained suppressions
- [ ] Remaining findings are tracked as issues

### Hints
- Refactor in two steps: first change structure with no behaviour change, then change behaviour.
- If a refactor has no test protecting it, write the test first.
- A good review comment says what, why and a suggestion.

```md
## Data access
- [ ] Every EF query receives the request's CancellationToken
- [ ] Read queries use AsNoTracking and project to DTOs
- [ ] TODO: add your own
```

### Common mistakes
- Huge "cleanup" commits mixing many changes.
- Turning off analyzers instead of fixing the code.
- Refactoring untested code with no safety net.

### Stretch (optional)
- Ask a friend to review one PR with your checklist and compare findings.

### Check your understanding
- What is on your checklist that a linter cannot check?
- How do you refactor safely?
- Which finding surprised you most?

days.learn: Writing a README recruiters read: problem, features, stack, how to run
days.title: README with screenshots, live link, run instructions and test commands
days.doneWhen: Someone else (or you, in a fresh folder on another machine) goes from clone to a running app with `docker compose up` using only the README, which has screenshots with alt text, the live link, the CI badge, test commands and links to the architecture docs
days.brief:
### Why this matters
A recruiter gives your repo about thirty seconds; an engineer at a product company gives it maybe five minutes. The README decides whether they look further. It should answer, in order: what problem this solves, what it looks like, what it is built with, how to run it, and how it is tested. Everything else lives one link away in the docs you wrote this week.

### What you'll build
- A rewritten root `README.md`:
  - one-sentence pitch and the problem it solves
  - a live link and the CI badge (week 20) at the top
  - three to five screenshots or a short GIF (board drag, live update across tabs, dashboard), each with alt text
  - a features list grouped by user value, not by technology
  - a stack section: .NET 10 minimal APIs, EF Core and SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, Hangfire, SignalR, React 19, TypeScript, TanStack Query, React Router, Playwright, Docker, GitHub Actions, Azure
  - "Run it locally": prerequisites, copy `.env.example` to `.env`, `docker compose up`, the URL, a demo login
  - "Tests": the one root command, plus E2E, with what each layer covers (link `TESTING.md`)
  - links to `docs/architecture.md`, the ADRs, `SECURITY.md` and `PERFORMANCE.md`
- Screenshots stored in `docs/images` at a sensible size

### Step by step
1. Read three READMEs of popular open source apps you admire. Note what you read first and what you skipped.
2. Write the pitch: who is it for and what does it do, in one sentence.
3. Capture screenshots from the live app with realistic demo data, not "test test".
4. Write run instructions, then follow them yourself in a new folder with a fresh clone. Fix every step that was not written down.
5. Keep it scannable: short sections, lists, no walls of text.
6. Add a "What I would do next" section linking the open issues from Wednesday.
7. Ask a friend to try it, or time yourself from clone to running app.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Clone to running app works from the README alone
- [ ] The live link and CI badge are at the top
- [ ] Every image has meaningful alt text
- [ ] Features are described by what users get
- [ ] No secrets or personal data in screenshots

### Hints
- Put the most impressive thing (live board updates across two tabs) in the first image.
- A demo account seeded only in the demo environment saves reviewers from registering.
- Relative links between docs work on GitHub and keep working in forks.

```md
# JobHunt
Track every job application from first contact to offer, live across all your devices.

[Live demo](https://...) · ![CI](...badge url...)
<!-- TODO: screenshot with alt text, features, stack, run, tests, docs -->
```

### Common mistakes
- Starting with installation steps before saying what the app is.
- Screenshots of empty states with no data.
- Run instructions that only work on your machine.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a short "Architecture in 60 seconds" section with the C4 level 2 diagram.

### Check your understanding
- What should a reader learn in the first ten seconds?
- How did you prove the run instructions work?
- What did you leave out of the README, and where does it live?

days.learn: Telling the story in interviews: trade-offs, failures, what you would change
days.title: 2-minute demo video and a one-page interview story sheet
days.doneWhen: Release v1.0.0 is published on GitHub with notes, a 2-minute demo video is linked from the README, and a one-page story sheet holds five interview stories, each practised aloud in under two minutes
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Building it was half the job; telling the story gets you hired. Interviewers ask "tell me about a project", "what was hard", "what would you change". Answers built on real trade-offs, failures and numbers from JobHunt beat any memorised answer. A short demo video lets people see the product without running anything.

### What you'll build
- A 2-minute screen recording: problem (10 s), main journey on the live app (60 s), one technical highlight such as live updates across two tabs or the 409 recovery (30 s), architecture slide (20 s)
- `docs/story-sheet.md`, one page, five stories in situation, task, action, result form:
  - the refresh token race and the shared refresh promise (week 8)
  - lost updates and rowversion with 409 (week 10)
  - the dual-write problem and the outbox (week 17)
  - a measured performance fix with numbers (weeks 12 and 21)
  - a failure: something that broke, how you found it (logs, traces, a flaky test) and what you changed
- A "what I would change" paragraph and a list of next steps:
  - a purge job that hard-deletes soft-deleted applications and their files
  - ETag and `If-Match` with 412 as an HTTP-native alternative to the version field
  - `HybridCache` replacing the hand-written cache-aside helper
  - the React Compiler, measured against the week 12 profiling
  - an active sessions list with revoke per device (week 8 stretch)
- Release v1.0.0: tag `v1.0.0` on main and a GitHub release with notes grouped by feature

### Step by step
1. Write the video script first, word for word, and time it.
2. Prepare demo data and two browser windows side by side. Hide bookmarks and notifications.
3. Record, watch once, re-record the worst part. Do not aim for perfect.
4. Write each story in five or six lines. Lead with the problem, end with a number or a lesson.
5. Practise each story out loud twice with a timer. Cut whatever you stumble over.
6. Tag the release and write the notes; link the video and the docs.
7. Merge the release branch, update the README with the video link, and share it.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The video is under two minutes and shows the live app
- [ ] Five stories, each with a trade-off or a number
- [ ] At least one honest failure story
- [ ] Next steps are specific and justified
- [ ] v1.0.0 is tagged and released

### Hints
- Interviewers probe the edges: "what if two tabs refresh at once?", "what if RabbitMQ is down?". Your ADRs hold the answers.
- Saying "I would do this differently now, because..." shows growth, not weakness.
- Keep the story sheet next to you in remote interviews, but do not read from it.

```md
## The refresh race
Situation: short access tokens, many parallel queries.
Problem: TODO
Action: TODO
Result: TODO (one number or one lesson)
```

### Common mistakes
- A 10-minute video nobody finishes.
- Stories that describe technology instead of decisions.
- No failure story, which sounds less believable, not more.

### Stretch (optional)
- Write a blog post on one ADR and link it from the README.

### Check your understanding
- What is the one trade-off you would mention first, and why?
- What would you change if you started again?
- How would you scale JobHunt to 100 times the users?

days.title: Whiteboard the full JobHunt architecture (browser to database, including events, cache and jobs) in 10 minutes
days.brief:
### The drill
Whiteboard the full JobHunt architecture (browser to database, including events, cache and jobs) in 10 minutes, then walk through two request flows out loud, in 20 minutes total.

### Rules
- Part 1 (10 minutes): blank whiteboard or paper, no notes, no docs, timer running.
- Part 2 (about 10 minutes): trace two flows on your drawing out loud, as if to an interviewer.
- This is a final exam: do the first attempt with nothing open, then compare with `docs/architecture.md` and note what you missed.
- No AI assistants.

### Must include
- Part 1: browser SPA, nginx, API layers (Api, Application, Domain, Infrastructure), SQL Server, Redis (cache, output cache store, backplane), RabbitMQ, Hangfire, Blob storage, SMTP, the trace collector
- Part 1: where auth happens: access token in memory, refresh cookie, hub token in the query string
- Part 2, flow 1: dragging a card to a new status: optimistic update, PATCH with version, 409 or 422 paths, commit with the outbox row, SignalR push to other tabs, cache updates
- Part 2, flow 2: the event's life after commit: outbox publisher, RabbitMQ, idempotent consumer, activity entry, feed, weekly digest job
- One sentence each on how it scales out and what you would add first

### Self-check
- [ ] Finished the drawing within 10 minutes
- [ ] Every arrow had a label
- [ ] You covered events, cache and jobs without prompting
- [ ] Both flows included a failure path
- [ ] You know exactly which parts you missed and where they are documented

### If you got stuck
- C4 diagrams and ADRs: redo Monday.
- Performance numbers: redo Tuesday.
- Code quality: redo Wednesday.
- README and run instructions: redo Thursday.
- Interview stories: redo Friday, then revisit the weeks behind any story you could not tell.
